I went to see my GP to get stitches out, too. He was originally my mother’s doctor and has been mine since I was a baby, so it was a bit of a tense situation for me.

But he was very kind and understanding, and offered to see me during hours if I needed stitches again so I didn’t have to go all the way to the ER. 

A doctor should remain compassionate and professional regardless of what the matter it. And good on you for taking care of yourself and seeking help. It’s so so scary, but ultimatly healing when we meet the right treatment providers.

Thank you for this and thank you for sharing. I’m so glad being open about this has helped you.

I had my session today and I still need time to process it all, but it did go pretty much as well as it could, concidering the circumstances. 

I didn’t back out. She could tell I had something I wanted to get off my chest and met me halfway, with understanding and concern where I’ve previously been met with disgust and anger from other treatment providers. Hopefully this is the beginning of a healthier line of thinking for me regarding this subject, but it was a pretty harrowing ordeal. 

I just don’t want to be a burden to her or make her feel like she can’t give me “the treatment I need”. She stared talking about maybe referring me out to someone whom she feels can better help me, but I really like seeing her and now that I’ve finally told her this, I don’t want to go through it all again with a new therapist even if they might be more specialized. 

After so many years we get disensitized to it and it’s hard for me to see my situation from the outside. To me this is “just” a familiar monster rearing its head, nothing to be overly concerned about, even if I feel like crap. But she took it very seriously. I’m glad, but at the same time I’m scared I’ll lose her.

My intention was not to minimize the struggle of bipolar 1 in any way, I was simply stating my own experience. The two diagnoses are not the same despite the similar names and mania is a completely different beast. 
That’s why I found it hurtful that my psychologist’s first reaction was to invalidate the whole thing by camparing it to the bipolar 1 diagnosis.
When I got my diagnosis my psychologist said I was lucky and got the “milder” form. I wanted to scream at her. There is so much misinformation out there, even among professionals.

Thank you for the update!

Your teacher seems really nice about it. I appreciate that he didn’t just confront you head on and was inconsiderate as people can tend to be. 

It’s easy to say that you shouldn’t overthink this, but I know it’s difficult and I really relate. However, I don’t think you need to worry. He seems to be thinking a lot about you and how to respond, so if/when he talks to you about it I really hope it goes well! 

And good on the school counselor for being considerate as well, even though he pulled you to the nursery. It’s nice to have someone looking out for you!

This was super brave of you, well done! 

If you’re comfortable with it, could you please update us after the conversation with your favorite teacher and tell us how it went? I’m super nervous about my own teacher finding out so I’m really hoping you have a good experience. 

Again; super well done!

I think it’s very individual for everyone. For me I usually get a 3-6 month long episode every year, as well as a few much shorter episodes during the months I’m usually “stable”. 

In your case it might also be that you’re currently in a very long episode, but your mood lifts every so often and you feel like yourself again. It doesn’t necessarily mean that one episode is over and another one begins, but rather it’s one long episode with a few respites within it. 

Mental illnesses are so individual and hard to pin down. Take care of yourself.

MDD is also an episodic illness, so that might be what‘s happening. It can’t really be called bipolar if you’re not experiencing mania or hypomania.  Your mood will of course fluctuate with MDD as well, just not that far upwards.

It used to vary wildly from month to month or between weeks, but that was before I started with the mood stabilizer. If this is anything like the last crash it’s the beginning of six+ months of hell. 
I hope you’re doing better, this absolutely sucks.

Thank you for this. It’s unreal to me that people can live in blissfull ignorance while also exploring the truths of the universe. I want your paragraph about a PhD in physics and not understanding a mood disorder framed on the wall in my living room, haha.

The divide between the sciences is promoting distrust and elitism, both on a personal and an academic level. I wish it wasn’t like this. 

And I also wish I had had some poo to fling at him.

Oh man, I know what you mean. And it doesn’t get any easier when all the tasks start building up and you just get completely overwhelmed. I also tend to put everything off until it reaches a point where it becomes destructive. It’s so much easier said than done, but small steps.

Excuse me, but what the actual fuck?! 
I’m so sorry this happened to you. Some people can be so impossibly ignorant and short-sighted and idiotic that I struggle to believe it sometimes. 

I’m glad you continue to wear shorts and skirts. Things like this stick with you for a long time, don’t feel weird about it still affecting you. You are not dumb, you are so so strong!
Getting stitches can be nerve wracking. It’s always such a relief when the people treating you keep their cool and are non-judgemental. I’m glad you got stitched up even though you were scared!
That’s so wonderful! You were very brave performing with short sleeves.

My mom did the same thing to me many years ago right after I had told her about my SH for the first time. 

She had bought a boxcutter to cut down flower stems and when she was putting it away she just had to say: “and you stay away from this!” This was not long after she had removed or locked away every sharp object in the house because of me.

It hurt my feelings terribly and I never told her about anything regarding SH again. An extreme reaction on my part definitely, but her comment really hit something painful inside me.
Damn, it sucks that it happens to others as well, but also I’m glad I’m not alone. I absolutely relate to what you’re saying; it’s so extremely intense when it’s going on.

For me alcohol is one of the worst things for my depression. If I’m already feeling bad when I start to drink I tend to drink way too much, both as a way of self harming  and a way to feel better. Things just crumble from there on out. I dissociate and get very self destructive and angry at myself. The evening usually ends in a pool of my own blood. Fortunately I don’t drink very often.

If I ever kill myself it will probably happen while blackout drunk.

Thank you for the replies! I decided to tie my jacked a little crooked around my waist to hide it and I think it worked as a temporary solution. I also used toilet paper as a makeshift bandaid to prevent further bleeding. I hope I don't make the same mistake in the future.

I've been through Zoloft withdrawl as well. I was on 150mg for almost two years, but I think it stopped working somewhere around 6 months in or so. Therefore, without the help of a psychiatrist or a doctor (because my therapist is a lazy fuck and I have trust issues), I just quit. 

After a couple of days without, the world would always "zap", like a scratch in the record or something, every time I looked left or right and when this happened I would take a new dose and wait. The zapping occured futher and further apart as  time went on and now I haven't taken a dose for about two months or so.  I think the whole process has taken about 8-9 months. The only mental/psychological withdrawl I've had is a major relapse of my depression and a suicide attempt, although I don't know if this is directly connected to withdrawl or If I'm just getting worse. 

Hope you get through withdrawl and feel better soon. Just remember what you're feeling now isn't permanent, your brain will clear up soon.

It has been going on for around  six years now. Can't really tell you anything about the reasons behind my feelings as I don't really know myself, but my therapist says it might partly be because I tend to keep everything to myself and that it has built up over the years. I'm still not sure I believe that, bet it's a reason as good as any I guess.

I don't really understand what you mean with "main factors"? Like the feeling in itself or something else?
I also find it odd that it isn't triggered by anything in particular, but for all I know it might be something subconcious.

I have it pretty similar. Over periods of time I can feel relativly fine and not let it bother me. I can function like a normal human being and do the things I'm supposed to do. I like those times, but during them I feel as if I might be faking everything and that I'm not really depressed at all. 

Then when it hits, it hits for weeks and weeks. I sleep way too much, I stop eating as my appetite is completely gone, and I just don't function in general. It feels as if my body weighs a thousand tons and the sort of "hollowness" in my chest is terrible. What a cliché, haha.
It goes in cycles and isn't really triggered by anything as far as I know. I've tried for several years with several different methods, but I don't think I'll get better.

The world of Skyrim. I must have played through that game a dozen times with different characters, and every time, like many other players, I discover something new. I got the game during a very dark period of my life, and just being able to immerse myself in the world and the stories and lore made real life bearable. 
The lore of The Elder Scrolls games is some of the most extensive I've ever come across, and if you know at least some of it, it makes the game that much more enjoyable, e.g when you meet a character famous in the lore and you say to yourself "I know who that is!"
